Police found a deceased person with multiple stab wounds inside a building in Queens on Friday, officials said.
The NYPD said officers entered a building at 3617 164 St. in Flushing around 4:30 p.m. on Friday and found an unconscious and unresponsive female individual.
Emergency responders pronounced her dead at the scene.
There were no arrests as of Friday night, and police hadn't yet described any suspects. Police also had not identified the woman or provided an estimate of her age. Police said the incident was still under investigation.

Amtrak’s proposal to rebuild Penn Station could lead to heaps of taxpayer money being used to subsidize a new entertainment venue for the Madison Square Garden Company.
The plan to overhaul the station calls for Amtrak to purchase the Infosys Theater at MSG, demolish it and convert the site into a grand light-filled entrance on Eighth Avenue. Previous estimates have put the cost of purchasing the theater at hundreds of millions of dollars.
During an investor’s call Wednesday, MSG’s chief financial executive David Collins fielded questions about the potential sale of the theater, which has a capacity for roughly 5,600 people. He noted the move would take away a revenue source for the company — but said the money from the sale could be used to fund a new venue, potentially in the five boroughs.
“The primary way for us to minimize the tax leakage would be to reinvest all of the potential proceeds in another domestic venue. … I would say that we are not limited to just the New York City market,” Collins said. “However, I would also say that New York City is our core operating market and with us having one less theater here, we would definitely most likely look to the New York market first.”
He did not say whether the Garden would look to buy an existing venue or build a new one.
In recent years James Dolan, the billionaire owner of MSG and the New York Knicks, has struck gold with his Las Vegas Sphere. That cutting-edge venue has a capacity for 20,000 people and has been so successful that Dolan is building another sphere at National Harbor on the Potomac River, just outside of Washington, D.C.
Amtrak special adviser Andy Byford, who is leading the redesign effort of Penn Station, has repeatedly said that the national railroad is looking to get us much money in federal grants and before potentially seeking funding from New York and New Jersey. That means if Amtrak's plan goes through, taxpayers would likely be on the hook to purchase the Infosys Theater — and in turn to fund MSG’s new theater elsewhere.
Representatives for MSG and Amtrak did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
MTA Chair Janno Lieber has repeatedly criticized Amtrak’s plan and has declined to sign on as an official partner for the rebuild, stating the work could interrupt Long Island Rail Road service at the station. Lieber has said Amtrak has refused to disclose the full details of its plan unless the New York transit agency agrees to join the project.
The MTA was planning its own rebuild of Penn Station — which is owned by Amtrak — until President Donald Trump took over the project last year. Lieber in 2023 said he did not want taxpayer money to be used to purchase the theater, saying he thought “the Dolans have gotten a pretty good deal from New Yorkers so far.”
While the MTA’s plan was under consideration that year, a private developer with ASTM Group estimated at a public hearing that the cost of purchasing Infosys was “substantially less” than $1 billion. The estimate came from Peter Cipriano, who is now CEO of Penn Transformation Partners, which was selected by the federal government to redevelop the rail hub.
Dolan supported Trump’s 2024 election campaign and this year backed Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman, who lost this week to Gov. Kathy Hochul.
MSG’s latest Securities and Exchange Commission filing lists the redevelopment of Penn Station as having a potential impact on its financial outlook, including the “potential transfer” of the Infosys Theater.
The Trump administration has set a tight deadline to begin work on the redevelopment of Penn Station. Officials said they expect shovels in the ground by the end of 2027.
Collins said during MSG’s investor call that executives “expect ample time to determine the appropriate path forward” on selling the theater.

A Flushing man has been indicted on charges including manslaughter after he allegedly sped past a stop sign while on cocaine and THC, then struck and killed a 1-year-old boy in a stroller.
Elvin Rivera, 57, was driving in a residential area of Flushing around 8:35 a.m. on Oct. 11 when he ran through a stop sign on 32nd Avenue, traveling northbound on Murray Street, according to the indictment.
He then sped through the intersection and struck the stroller, which was being pushed by the 1-year-old’s nanny, authorities say.
The Queens District Attorney’s Office said Rivera remained on the scene, where he failed drug sobriety and field tests. A blood test later confirmed the presence of THC and cocaine, the DA’s office said. Rivera had also been driving in violation of restrictions resulting from a DWI case in April, according to the DA’s office.
The child, 1-year-old Justin Hu, was rushed to the hospital, where he was later pronounced dead, according to Queens District Attorney Melinda Katz.
“Our thoughts are with Justin’s family as they mourn this unimaginable loss,” Katz said in a statement Friday.
The indictment charges Rivera with 12 counts, including manslaughter, vehicular manslaughter, assault, driving while impaired, failure to exercise due care and failing to stop at a sign.
He could face up to 15 years in prison if convicted of the top charge, and is scheduled to return back to court on Jan. 7.
Attorney information for Rivera was not immediately available.

A former rowing coach was arrested Thursday in the Bronx on allegations of sexual assault and rape stemming from his time coaching on Cape Cod, according to law enforcement officials.
Guy Monseair, 57, was taken into custody on City Island around 7 a.m. by officers from the NYPD and Homeland Security Investigations Human Trafficking Task Force, officials said. According to the Barnstable, MA Police Department, he is charged with four counts of aggravated statutory rape of a child and one count of indecent assault and battery on a child under 14.
Police said all of the alleged incidents took place between 2008 and 2011 while Monseair was a rowing coach at several different clubs on the Cape. Barnstable Police said they were made aware of the allegations last month.
It was not immediately clear when Monseair moved to the Bronx. NYPD officials said he started the City Island Rowing group between 2012 and 2014, though officials couldn’t say if he was still involved in the organization. There have not been any allegations against Monseair from his time in New York, according to the NYPD.
An undated online profile page lists Monseair as the head coach and executive director of City Island Rowing. The profile says that he grew up in Zimbabwe and moved to the U.S. to pursue his coaching career full time.
“At City Island Rowing, Monseair’s coaching philosophy emphasizes both athletic and personal growth, with a focus on resilience, teamwork, and discipline. Under his leadership, the program has grown to support a large team of athletes, many of whom have achieved national and collegiate success,” the page reads.
The organization did not immediately respond to several messages seeking comment.
In a statement, a spokesperson for USRowing said the organization revoked Monseair’s membership rights as soon as they learned about the allegations on Thursday. That means he is prohibited from participating in all competitions and activities under their jurisdiction.
USRowing also reported the matter to the U.S. Center for SafeSport, and urged other abuse survivors to come forward either online or by phone at 833-5US-SAFE (833-587-7233).
According to the Barnstable Police Department, Monseair will be extradited back to Massachusetts, where the case will be prosecuted by the Cape and Islands District Attorney's Office.
Information for his lawyer was not immediately available.
This is a developing story and was updated with new information.

This column originally appeared in On The Way, a weekly newsletter covering everything you need to know about NYC-area transportation.
Sign up to get the full version, which includes answers to reader questions, trivia, service changes and more, in your inbox every Thursday.
For three years, this newsletter and weekly radio segment on All Things Considered have dug into the nitty gritty of the subways and streets.
Now, much like an old A train getting upgraded to a sleek R211, we’re improving service for our audience. On The Way is launching an hour-long pop-up radio show on Thursdays. Starting next week, on Nov. 12, tune into WNYC 93.9 FM from 1 to 2 p.m., listen on the WNYC app, or check out our YouTube channel for the show hosted by me, Stephen Nessen. I’ll be speaking with my fellow transportation reporter Ramsey Khalifeh and editor Clayton Guse, bringing you analysis of the latest transportation news.
We’ll have special guests, including decision makers and the sharpest thinkers in the transit world. We’ll take your calls and welcome questions about your daily commutes, as well as your hopes and dreams for mass transit. Write me at [email protected].
It’s going to be a gas — consider this your invitation.
As we do in this newsletter each week, we’ll discuss the most important transportation topics of our time, from the redevelopment of Penn Station and the antiquated elements of the subway system, to the new projects like the Interborough Express and Penn Access. We’ll look at the ongoing issues in the transit system like fare evasion, subway signals, and the future of the taxi industry.
We’ll also look at the subway bottlenecks that slow your commutes, and share tips on how to legally avoid paying for the AirTrain, or navigate Exit 31 on the BQE without pulling your hair out.
Speaking of the BQE, you can bet we’ll get into that too.
The Curious Commuter segment will continue, so please keep the questions coming!
As always, we welcome your thoughts on our coverage on the web, on the air and in your inbox. Talk to you on the airwaves.
NYC transportation news this week
Bus and bike lanes galore to come. Advocates say that a ballot measure that passed on election night will reform the process for the construction of bus and bike lanes and means more street safety projects throughout the five boroughs. The measure will amend the city charter to “simplify the review of street safety projects to reduce construction timelines,” according to the text of the ballot question.
“This really just defangs some of the opponents who have sought to slow down and stop these street safety projects,” said Ben Furnas, executive director of Transportation Alternatives.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s office estimated construction timelines on major bus and bike lane projects could be reduced by at least 33%. But the measure still requires the city to solicit input from community boards before moving forward with any street redesign.
SoHo basketball court set to leave MTA construction purgatory. The refreshed Grand Canal Court at Sixth Avenue, set to open at the end of November, will feature new benches, a water fountain, upgraded lighting and fencing. The courts were originally ripped up in 2022 so workers could build a new substation that provides electricity to trains.
Scary good ridership for the MTA over Halloweekend. On Halloween Saturday, 3.27 million riders got on the subway, the most on a Saturday since 2016. And during the New York City Marathon, the subway saw its highest Sunday ridership on record.
NYPD seizes e-bikes along a clogged East Village street. Eleven e-bikes parked along East 11th Street and First Avenue were confiscated by police last week. Neighboring business owners and residents have been complaining for months about idle delivery bikes clogging sidewalks and curbs, sometimes by the hundreds.
Watchdog says MTA should eliminate some jobs to prepare for budget woes. The budget watchdog Citizens Budget Commission recommends the MTA should make sweeping cuts to positions that it argues technology has made obsolete as the agency could be looking at a nearly $900 million funding shortfall as spending outpaces fare revenue.
Curious Commuter
Have a question for us? Use this form to submit yours and we may answer it in a future newsletter!
Question from Charles in Brooklyn
Charles from Brooklyn asks: Why on earth did the MTA eliminate over half of the seats on the new D trains?! We have long commutes and need those seats!
Answer
The MTA has been slowly replacing some of the oldest subway cars (in lines like the A, C and now D) with new R211 trains. They’re noticeably different from the trains of yore with “ conversational” yellow-and-orange seats. The newer subway cars have wider doors to allow for more people to easily get on and off the trains. And yes, there are notably fewer seats. More standing room means more space for people in a single subway car than previous models with more seats. While riders with longer commutes have a lower chance of snagging a seat on one of these new train cars, the modern equipment is less likely to break down, meaning better service all around.

Google is locked in a standoff with the nation’s largest public school system as the debate over AI’s place in the classroom pits parent groups against the tech behemoth.
Earlier this week, Google said schools that ban artificial intelligence will lose access to Google search, prompting cries of blackmail and a swift rebuke from Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
“Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools,” Mamdani wrote on X. “No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children. Our public schools exist to serve students, not to grow the profit margins of Big Tech.”
In September, Mamdani announced a one-year ban on most AI programs in city schools and tighter limits on screens, especially for the youngest students. The moratorium was a major win for city parents who oppose the use of artificial intelligence in public school classrooms.
But Google’s threat to pull the plug on search in classrooms underscored how deeply the technology’s products are woven into the fabric of education.
Google products are ubiquitous in schools. Since the pandemic, many students have been issued individual Chromebooks for schoolwork and remote learning. City officials said the school system has 1.3 million Chromebooks, with about 500,000 assigned to students, and another 800,000 in schools. Teachers post assignments to Google Classroom, and students, like many adults, rely heavily on Google Docs and search.
“It would be incredibly difficult for us to disentangle our school system entirely from Google, and that's what they're betting on,” said Kelly Clancy, part of the coalition calling for a total ban on AI in the city’s public schools. She said all three of her children are required to use Google Classroom for remote learning and homework.
This is a perfect time for us to figure out how we wean ourselves off of Google so that we don't have companies able to blackmail us in order to create a captive audience of studentsKelly Clancy, who is part of a coalition calling for a total ban on AI in NYC schools.
“But I think what they're not counting on is the fact that parents across the country have mobilized against this,” Clancy said. “And this is a perfect time for us to figure out how we wean ourselves off of Google so that we don't have companies able to blackmail us in order to create a captive audience of students.”
Google has insisted it’s impossible to separate the company’s search function from AI.
Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told the New York Times that “search and A.I. are deeply integrated,” so turning off AI will also mean turning off the search engine. The company said the new policy would go into effect early next year. It did not respond to Gothamist’s requests for comment.
But over the past year, an influential movement of parents, educators and lawmakers have sought to beat back the creep of artificial intelligence in schools. They argue AI summaries and bots enable cheating, short-circuit learning and seduce children into inappropriate and even dangerous relationships. This week, parents of a North Carolina 13-year-old sued Google alleging she made plans to end her life after interacting with its AI Mode.
Education officials said they were still trying to figure out how Google’s new policy would affect search in schools.
Officials are “reaching out to Google to discuss this update further,” public schools spokesperson Nicole Brownstein said.
She said the city has disabled the Gemini chatbot and AI mode on Google Chromebooks issued to students, and they’ve made requests to Google to disable the AI Overview that continues to appear in search results.
“We will keep students and school communities updated as we continue to place student safety and wellbeing above all other interests,” she said.
Following the Times report, Google posted additional information about its plans on X.
It said the announcements give schools "more choice, not less" and that Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Google Search will be off by default, and schools will be in charge of which service, if any, is turned on.
The company emphasized the changes were made in response to feedback from K-12 schools. Google said it’s also changing how AI will function within search “to make it better for learning.” The company said both AI Mode and AI Overviews will offer step-by-step guidance through problems” rather than just “quick answers to schoolwork.”
Assemblymember Alex Bores noted that Google has made “deep investments” into its educational offerings over the years, aggressively and successfully marketing its suite of products to schools.
“This is a product choice that Google is making, and it's a profit maximizing one,” said Bores, who worked at Palantir and recently co-founded Who Decides, an advocacy group for AI safety and regulation.
“Competitors like Duck Duck Go let people opt in or opt out of AI search. And Google could do the same. They could also do the same only when it comes to children if they wanted. But they're making an intentional choice not to, and I think that's a disappointing one,” he said.

Construction workers discovered part of a 19th-century human skeleton behind a building in the West Village on Thursday, according to the NYPD.
Officials said a construction crew excavating the backyard of 79 Christopher St. called 911 around 11 a.m. after finding several bones and part of a skull, buried 4 to 7 feet below the ground.
The city medical examiner determined that the bones were historic, and likely buried when the plot of land was used as a cemetery for the neighboring church in the mid-1800s, according to the NYPD. The property is adjacent to St. John’s Lutheran Church, which dates back to 1855.
Police said no foul play was suspected, and that it was not immediately clear if the remains belonged to a woman or a man.
